```{r, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(knitr)
library(DBI)
library(RSQLite)
```

<!-- Excel and delimited files are designed for storing either small or mid-sized datasets. The large datasets are normally stored in databases and have  -->


You will very rarely see large datasets stored in Excel or delimited files. Instead, they are normally stored in relational databases. There are plenty of so-called database management systems -- a piece of software that allows communicating with databases. For example, you might hear of such database management systems as MySQL, MS SQL Server, MongoDB, etc. Luckily, R has a package that allows connecting to different databases with the same syntax. In this unit, we dive deep into how to import the data from databases into R.

### `{DBI}`

The package `{DBI}` could be the oldest package in this section: its core structure was implemented in 2003. The main idea of the package is to provide a common interface for various databases. By interface, we mean the way you interact and communicate with databases. In other words, regardless of the database you want to work with, your steps and used functions will be the same (or almost the same). It is possible due to a specific design: we will deal only with the front-end, and we do not have to worry about what happens behind the curtain -- the back-end. The back-end is those packages that are directly deal with databases, e.g., `{RSQLite}` for SQLite, `{RPostgres}` for PostgreSQL, etc. But we do not need to be familiar with all of these packages since they are used only by `{DBI}`.

There are three major steps in the process of interacting with the database: 

1. Open the connection to the database 
2. Interact with databases (i.e., retrieve table names, collect/harvest tables with data, etc.)
3. Close the connection 

Let's cover each step of this process. 

#### 1. Open the connection 

The function to set the connection with the database is `dbConnect()`. It is probably the only function that would require some tweaks in arguments, if you are working with different databases. We will focus on SQLite, but a similar logic can be applied to other types. SQLite stores the entire database as a single file, and if you are a macOS user, you do not need to install any software to interact with it.

Before we start, we need to install both the front-end `{DBI}` **and the back-end** `{RSQLite}`. For other databases, you will need to install other back-ends.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
install.packages("DBI")
install.packages("RSQLite")
```

We also will load them both before we use them:

```{r}
library(DBI)
library(RSQLite)
```

Now, we need to set up the connection. The function that we will use is `dbConnect()`. The first argument of this function is always a so-called driver. The driver is the object that defines what kind of database will be used. In our case, it is `SQLite()`, but if you would use MySQL, it should be `MySQL()` from `{RMySQL}`, etc. 

The second argument in our case is a path to the file that contains the database. For other databases, you will probably need to provide other things, like `host`, `port`, etc. But let's get back to our SQLite case:

```{r}
connection <- dbConnect(
  SQLite(), 
  "data/company.db"
)
```

Hey, we have just established a connection between two distinct tools, isn't that cool? 

#### 2. Interact with databases

The connection has been set, but so far we do not have the data in our hands (or better say R's hands). The connection is simply a channel through which R can communicate with the database. Like a telephone cable that connects you and the person on the other side of the phone. Now it is time to talk with the database. 

The database is not just a single table, but a collection of tables. You can think about tables as of R tibbles, they are very similar concepts. These tables have their own names and can be accessed by R by their names. Therefore, the first natural thing to do is to check which tables we have in the database: 

```{r}
dbListTables(connection)
```

Once you have these names, it is time to read the content of tables into R. We will show you only the crude approach for now, which can be applied to relatively small non-industrial databases. You need to use a slightly different method when dealing with large tables, and we will come back to this in the data wrangling part. For now, we will operate with two functions: `tbl()` and `collect()`.

```{r}
customers <- tbl(connection, "customers") %>% collect()
```

They have to be called consecutively (i.e., via the pipe), so that the result of `tbl()` is passed to `collect()`. As in the case of `dbListTables()`, the first argument is the connection between R and database. Then, we have to specify which table from the database we want to work with (it should be provided as a character vector). The function `tbl()` will create a new connection (yes, another one), but this time directly with the database table. When we specifying `collect()` -- we directly import this table into R memory. 

By the way, `customers` on the left before `<-` can be anything, it is just a name of the variable. It does not have to coincide necessarily with the name of the table in the database, but this is a good idea to name it similarly.

When this command is executed, you can treat `customers` as a normal tibble. 


#### 3. Close the connection 

It is important to close the connection, once we retrieve all the data we wanted to. It is like using your stove: you switch it on, boil some water, and then switch it off. The stove has two or four burners, so there is a limited number of persons can use it at the same time. So switching it off is necessary because you will give access to the stove to the other member of your household. The same happens with the database -- it has a limited bandwidth and a limited number of users.

You can easily close the connection with the following command: 

```{r}
dbDisconnect(connection)
```

Once you closed the connection, you cannot use it anymore to get load tables to R. If you want to continue interacting with the database, you will need to establish a brand new connection. 

```{r, echo=FALSE}
knitr::include_graphics("slides/slides.001.png")
```

### Exercises

In this set of exercises, we will cover all three steps that have seen before. We will import the data from the database dedicated to Futurama (a popular sci-fi adult cartoon from the 2000s). You can find the database file `futurama.db` in the `data` folder.

In the data science world, it is very common not to have any prior information about the data you will work with, for instance, the architecture of the database. 

<!-- We will try to replicate these circumstances.  -->

* Connect to the database. We wrote a small example and you just need to fill in the blank spots that are denoted by `________`.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
library(________)
library(________)


connection <- dbConnect(
  SQLite(),
  "________"
)
```

**Solution:**

```{r}
library(DBI)
library(RSQLite)


connection <- dbConnect(
  SQLite(),
  "data/futurama.db"
)
```

* Print out the names of the tables in the database. How many tables do we have? 

**Solution:**

```{r, eval=TRUE}
dbListTables(connection)
```

```{r, eval=TRUE}
dbListTables(connection) %>% length()
```

* What was the very first word pronounced in this series? To answer this question, you need to look at the content of each table and guess which one we need to use.

**Hint:** The first word will be in the first row of the transcripts.

**Solution:**

```{r}
episodes <- tbl(connection, "episodes") %>% collect()
episodes
```

```{r}
transcripts <- tbl(connection, "transcripts") %>% collect()
transcripts
```

The word is `r transcripts %>% pull(line) %>% first() %>% str_split(" ") %>% first() %>% first()`.

* Another useful skill that we will train right now is to look for a function, even if you do not know its name. If a package you work with is more or less consistent, you can hope to find this function without googling. 

Let's try to retrieve the column names without importing the full table (e.g., it could be too large). A couple of facts that can help you to guess the function name: (1) Since we want to retrieve a list of column names, we could hope to have a similar function name to `dbListTables()`; (2) columns are called fields in database context; (3) many functions from `{DBI}` start with `db`. One more useful hint: you can type a couple of first letters of the function in the console and press <kbd>Tab</kbd>. 

When you have guessed the name of the function, you can type `?name_of_function` to see its documentation. Please read it carefully and try to apply this function to one of the tables of your choice. 

**Solution:**

```{r, eval=FALSE}
?dbListFields
```

```{r}
dbListFields(connection, "episodes")
```

* Close the database connection. 

**Solution:**

```{r}
dbDisconnect(connection)
```

---

As a final word, we did not dive deep into database and R communication. However, even with this simple set of tools, you can import tables from databases.
